# Reproducing images (woodcut, engraving, etching, lithography) (`lithography_engraving`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by paper, printing_press, nitric_acid, copper_bronze
- Core idea: Woodcut: lines left in relief on a block, printed with type in the same press. Copper engraving and etching: lines cut with a burin, or bitten by acid through a wax ground scratched with a needle; ink is rubbed into the grooves and wiped off the surface, and a roller press forces damp paper into the lines. It gives far finer detail, for maps and technical drawings. Lithography (1796): draw with a greasy crayon on fine-grained limestone, wet the stone, and greasy ink sticks only to the drawing; no cutting, so any artist can draw directly. Halftone screens (1880s) break photographs into dots that print with type.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying to print an intaglio plate in the letterpress with the text: it needs a separate roller press and a second pass
  - Forgetting that every image must be drawn reversed
  - Expecting copper plates to last indefinitely: they wear after a few thousand impressions unless re-cut or steel-faced
  - Etching with strong acid in a closed room: the fumes are dangerous
  - Using any stone for lithography: it needs a fine, even, porous limestone like Solnhofen's
- History: china: 868 – woodcut frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra; 1633 Ten Bamboo Studio colour prints from multiple blocks; east_asia: 1765 – Japanese full-colour woodblock prints (nishiki-e, Harunobu); europe: c. 1430s – copper engraving by goldsmiths in Germany; 1481 Florentine Dante with engravings after Botticelli (Baccio Baldini); c. 1500 etching (Daniel Hopfer); 1796–1798 Senefelder's lithography; 1837 chromolithography (Engelmann); 1882 Meisenbach's halftone; 1904 offset printing
- Read:
  - William M. Ivins Jr., Prints and Visual Communication (1953)
  - Arthur M. Hind, A History of Engraving and Etching (1923)
  - Alois Senefelder, A Complete Course of Lithography (1819)
